newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain threatens travel ban against Cuba.
newsitem.headline: Spain threatens travel ban against Cuba.

text.p: Spain, angered by Cuba's jailing of a Spanish tourist after a minor traffic accident, threatened on Wednesday to warn its citizens to stay away from the communist-ruled island.

In the latest diplomatic dispute between the two countries, Spanish Foreign Minister Abel Matutes told state radio: "This situation is intolerable and Spain is going to use all of its resources and those of its European partners to get his immediate release and return to Spain."
Matutes said the Spanish government was considering issuing a travel advisory for Cuba, a popular holiday destination for Spaniards.
He said the tourist, 30-year-old Jesus Martin, was jailed after a minor car accident a month ago and was still in custody.
But in Havana, the Spanish consul said Martin was held for only one night but was prevented by police from leaving Cuba pending trial.
According to Spanish journalists Consul Eduardo Cerro said the incident was not as serious as originally reported and appeared to stem from a lack of coordination between judges and police.
Martin, speaking to state radio from Cuba, said he had been asked to pay for damages and had been imprisoned when he could not immediately come up with the money.

Matutes said the case was "strange" because the car Martin was driving was insured and there were no injuries and only a small amount of damage. The minister said he thought Martin had been the victim of a ruse to get money.
He said Spain was considering bringing action against Cuba because of what he called its "absolute lack of judicial controls".
"We are studying the possibility, given this lack of guarantees, to recommend that Spanish citizens not travel to Cuba," he said.
Matutes said the Cuban embassy had assured him Martin's case was being handled in the courts. "It's in the hands of a judge, but we all know how these things are in some countries," he said.
Relations between Cuba and Spain have soured since the conservative government of Jose Maria Aznar took over last May after 13 years of Socialist rule in Spain.

Aznar's Popular Party government, the first right-wing administration since the fascist dictatorship of Francisco Franco ended in 1975, has taken a harder line against Cuba and encouraged the European Union to do so as well.

The EU, at Spain's urging, pledged in December to push for democracy in Cuba. It said it would consider negotiating a trade and cooperation agreement with Cuba but said such a pact could be suspended if there was a serious breach of human rights.
Tension between Spain and Cuba rose last November when Havana accepted and then withdrew approval for a new Spanish ambassador, accusing Spain of interfering in its internal affairs.
Spain's Socialist opposition criticised the government on Wednesday for what it said was overreaction.

"Such a disproportionate reaction dangerously elevates a personal matter to a diplomatic level," Socialist spokesman Luis Yanez told Reuters. "It stems from the tense relations between Cuba and Spain but the Ministry should show more prudence."
